title.en: Covalent bonding and versatile nature of carbon

text.en: Coal, diamond, wood, petrol and food are all made of carbon compounds. Why is this one element so special?

Carbon has four valence electrons, so it cannot easily lose or gain four. Instead it shares electrons in covalent bonds.
In methane CH4, carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogens. Covalent compounds usually have low melting and boiling points and are poor conductors.
Carbon shows catenation, the ability to form long chains, branched chains and rings by bonding with itself.
Carbon's valency of four lets it bond with many other atoms, such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine.
Saturated compounds have only single bonds, like alkanes CnH2n+2. Unsaturated compounds have double (alkenes CnH2n) or triple (alkynes CnH2n-2) bonds.
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group where each member differs from the next by CH2.
A functional group is an atom or group that decides the properties, such as -OH in alcohols, -COOH in carboxylic acids, -CHO in aldehydes and >C=O in ketones.
Naming: choose the longest chain, use the prefix meth-, eth-, prop-, but-; the ending -ane, -ene, -yne; for alcohols -ol and for acids -oic acid.
